Course Overview
This is the companion website for HEKA22 Ecological Economics at Lund University, VT26.

Learning Objectives






TipBy the end of this course you should:



Demonstrate the ability to independently apply anthropological, historical, sociological, and economic perspectives to environmental issues,

demonstrate the ability to convey in-depth knowledge of human ecology in both spoken and written communication,
demonstrate the ability to conduct subject-related information searches, evaluate information, and master reference management.
demonstrate the ability to engage in informed discussion of the relationship between environmental problems and economic growth,

Assignments
The final assignment for this course is an essay answering one of these questions:

Formulate a question you found difficult to answer previously, but now have the tools to reason around. Tie your answer to theory, practice, and concrete examples.
Choose one economic school of thought to answer the following. Based on the course’s material and discussions, argue how your everyday behavior can contribute to “a safe and just place for all within planetary boundaries”. How can microeconomics and micropolitics influence larger systems? Use theory, praxis and examples to deepen your analysis.
Karl Polanyi’s work shows how tightly the economy, culture and society are intertwined. How have your own social and cultural background and experience formed your view on the economy? Point thoroughly to theories from the course to support your reflection.
During the course you encountered concepts (for example, “green growth”, “Doughnut economics”, “Degrowth”) that propose different ways for the economy to respond to environmental issues. Chose one of these frames, explain its position and then criticize another frame from it.
Propose your own question to me, if it fits the frame of the course and the learning objectives, you may write about something you are passionate about.

Instructions: Write a 3000–4000 word essay with a clear structure, consisting of an introduction, a main body with well-developed paragraphs, and a conclusion. Cite correctly, following the department’s citation style. The library offers substantial support (use them!). Your arguments need to be coupled to the lectures, seminars, and assigned readings for this course. You are free to use additional material.
You may write this in English, or Swedish.

Using Computers and AI
Computers and AI are great tools and for better and worse there is no way around using them anymore. But you should be mindful about when they add to your learning and when they subtract from it.
I strongly encourage you to leave your computers—anything with a screen really—in your bags during class. Use pen and paper in class, then add a digital summary if you want to. It will help you stay focused and, more importantly, help others not to get distracted by whatever you would be doing on your screen. If you must use a screen, please find a seat at the back of the room.
I will not tell you what you should and should not use AI for; as long as it improves your learning outcomes. However, I think there are some elements you should consider. Since LLM’s entered mainstream use their abilities have grown tremendously. They can now carry out very complex tasks with high quality results. Making those decisions is an experience-based skill. But it still requires human knowledge and intervention to ultimately decide what is true, useful, effective, beautiful. The bad news: nobody is born with it, it is a skill that needs to be developed. Developing it requires annoying experimentation, failing and trying again and again, and reflexivity to develop. The good news: because of that it is something that will make you stand out if you have developed it.
You can use LLM’s to develop those skills too. They can even be extremely helpful for this: you can use them as a tutor testing your knowledge, or as peers to whom you explain concepts you are learning, or as guides helping you understand dense academic text by rephrasing it. But your learning success will depend on the same factors as with all other learning activities:

Make a plan of what you want to understand: what do you think will happen? Did it happen? Why, why not? Applied to AI: before asking the AI think about what you believe the answer will be. Was it?
Spacing is better than cramming: LLM’s generate a lot of text—fast. This can make it tempting to rush from topic to topic, question to question, but your brain needs time to memorize. Active recall—where you try to actively remember information instead of just passively consuming—spaced out over time is the key to remembering things. Applied to AI: take frequent breaks; ask it to quiz you on something you learned yesterday, or last week. Do not just reread old text passively.
Actively integrate new knowledge with what you already know. Test yourself to identify gaps in your knowledge. Try to fill them. Then test yourself again.

The central element in all of this is using your brain actively not just passively consuming information.

title: 1  Introduction to Ecological Economics
text:
2.1 Mainstream and Heterodox Economics
In the wake of the global financial crisis in 2008, calls grew louder to pluralize economics—that is to make the study of how humans make a living more open to different perspectives than formal, mathematical models which mimic mechanical physics. These efforts were successful in some respects and failed in others. If you walk into an “Econ 101” lecture at virtually any university in the world you will likely be met by very similar content, mathematical symbols and diagrams taught from a small range of accepted text books.
At the same time, many researchers now draw on a much wider toolkit than even a decade ago—and are recognized for it! The most recent Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences went to scholars deeply engaged in, for example, Evolutionary Economics (Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt), Institutional Economics (Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson in 2024) or Behavioral Economics (Richard H. Thaler in 2017). There are a number of flaws with the so-called Nobel Prize in Economics and—with the exception to Thaler these economist—would likely reject the notion of being called heterodox, their works draw on and speak to mainstream economics to a larger extent, but it illustrates that economics is a diverse field, with many different approaches, methods, and research topics.
A great overview of this diversity can be found at exploring-economics.org or in the book Rethinking Economics (Fischer et al. 2017). I highly suggest you spend some time there to explore the broad range, different ontologies (assumptions about what the social world is) and epistemologies (assumptions about how we can know it).
Figure 2.1 shows just one way of making sense of the field: by looking at the problem each approach views as central. As you can see, Ecological Economics has some overlap with other approaches in viewing scarcity, uncertainty, and change as central economic problems.






Figure 2.1: Overview of Economic Subfields from exploring-economics.org




2.1.1 What is Mainstream Economics?
The fields listed on exploring economics can all be viewed as part of mainstream economics, to the extent that they use key concepts which economics students are taught in their first semesters. These include self-regulating markets, firms and households, supply and demand, price formation, the allocation of resources, equilibrium, efficiency and optimality (Røpke 2020).
In addition to the different fields in economics, you will often find two terms to describe the level of analysis in economics: macro- and microeconomics.
In short, the macroeconomics analyzes the economy in is aggregated form, usually at the level of nations. Typical questions are, for example, how much economic activity happens in a given country, such as Sweden? How much do prices increase, and where do people find employment?
Microeconomics on the other hand studies the behavior of individual agents—usually people or firms—although other levels are possible too, such as households. Typical questions here involve how do firms decide what and how much to produce? How do changes in price affect the purchasing behavior of consumers?

title: 1  Introduction to Ecological Economics
section: 2.2 The core tension: How do we overcome the mainstream economic paradigm?
text:
2.2 The core tension: How do we overcome the mainstream economic paradigm?
Is Ecological Economics a real alternative to mainstream economics, or has it become co-opted, in other words taken over or absorbed, by mainstream economics?
There are three broadly recognized streams within ecological economics that differ in the extent to which they engage with, draw on, and sympathize with mainstream economics.
To understand the different streams within ecological economics, we will use a puzzle created by Dallaire-Fortier, Dwarkasing, and Plomteux (no date). You can find all materials and the “solution” to the puzzle in the materials at the linked website.
Use this overview to reflect on your own position: For example, does your view on the economy align with one of the three paradigms more than the others? How do you think Ecological Economics should balance fundamentally replacing the mainstream economics paradigm with using tools and theories from it?

text: 4.1 Learning Objectives

title: 4  Raw Materials and Metabolism
text:
Describe the material throughput of modern economies, including the distinction between domestic extraction and material footprint, and identify which world regions are net importers versus net exporters of embodied materials.
Analyze asymmetries in raw material consumption across countries and explain the mechanisms—historical, economic, and biophysical—that produce and sustain them.
Evaluate proposed strategies for reducing material throughput (decoupling, degrowth, circular economy) against empirical evidence on their feasibility.

title: 4  Raw Materials and Metabolism
text:
4.2 Peer Teaching
Today’s lecture is given by the students. This is to practice:

Reading with a purpose (extracting, transforming, and using information for communicative ends).
Retelling, informing, communicating (planning and delivering a lecture that presents the main arguments, points, and knowledge in a structured and clear way).
Collaboration.
Speaking in front of a group of peers.

Each person reads all assigned articles. Each group reads its assigned article especially carefully and jointly plans, structures, and delivers a lecture for the rest of the student group. The group also formulates a discussion question and submits it to me before the lecture.
At the peer-teaching lecture, you have 18 minutes at your disposal (including starting up any slides, writing on the board, or other preparations needed).
Tips and advice:

Get started early.
Feel free to read supporting literature, for example, cited sources, text books on the topic (Chapter 4 in Spash (2018)), Wikipedia pages.
Google expressions and theories so you understand them.
If the group work falls apart for one reason or another, let me know early!
